answer.rationale:
Constraints eliminate most of the inherited playbook before evidence even matters. memory_b1 (rollback) is the strongest-looking precedent and the timing is suggestive \u2014 latency began climbing 30 minutes after a release \u2014 but compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so that path is closed regardless of how well it worked on day 18. memory_b2 (regional failover) and memory_b4 (circuit breaker) both trade writes for latency recovery: failover mid-peak risks in-flight settlement writes and replication-lag divergence, and failing fast on the write path deliberately sheds the exact traffic the primary objective says not to lose. memory_b3 (add capacity) succeeded as pre-provisioning ahead of a known peak, not as a 90-minute-in mitigation; provisioning lead time likely exceeds the window we have. That leaves memory_b5, which is the only precedent that reduces primary write-path pressure without discarding writes, so I am spending the single verification pull there rather than on the more eye-catching rollback memory \u2014 verifying a memory I cannot act on buys nothing.

What I need from the archive is whether day 55's write-latency recovery was actually attributable to the replica routing or merely coincided with the promotional window ending, and how much of the primary's load was in fact read traffic. The consolidated summary asserts causation ('took load off the primary; write latency recovered the same day') that a same-day correlation would not establish. If the original record shows the read share was small, this intervention will not move a 5x p99 and I should fall back to capacity provisioning and accept that relief lands in the next window.

Important unresolved uncertainty: no memory here diagnoses the current cause. The release correlation is unexplained, and if the patch itself introduced write amplification or a lock-contention regression, offloading reads treats a symptom while the true driver keeps climbing. memory_b6 suggests canary cohorts would have surfaced a regression within an hour, and they evidently did not flag this one, which is itself weak evidence the release may not be the cause \u2014 but it is weak, and I am not treating it as settled.

Hence small_guarded_test rather than a broad cutover: shift only report and dashboard query classes, on a subset, with replica lag and error rates watched continuously and a fast revert path. Downstream value risk is real and I am flagging it \u2014 stale reads served from a lagging replica can feed reconciliation and settlement logic and corrupt figures that look authoritative later, so anything read-your-writes sensitive or settlement-critical stays pinned to the primary. If lag exceeds threshold, revert routing rather than widen it.
